theme_arguments.name: Marriage
arguments: Their marriage is utterly unique due to its theological origin as the only marriage untainted by sin.
A+E shown to be logical, considering the different interpretations of God's intentions.
Milton humanises A+E through psychological realism — realistic dialogue, linguistic nuance: grounds the biblical story in recognisable emotional experience.
Consciously echoes and critiques the marriage debates of the time, situating PL within a current and highly relevant time of political and theological discourse.

theme_arguments.name: Love
arguments: Love is a contributing factor to the fall and becomes a form of moral weakness.
Milton distinguishes between prelapsarian and postlapsarian love.

theme_arguments.name: Power
arguments: Power is primarily rhetorical — Eve is persuaded rather than overpowered.
Persuasion interacts with pre-existing desires: power coproduced between tempter and tempted.
Pursuit of power is fundamentally self-defeating.
Power does have real, albeit limited, effects.
Milton upholds the existence of true, absolute power in the form of divine authority.

theme_arguments.name: Gender
arguments: Milton encodes Eve's fall within a framework of gender hierarchy: morally corrupt and dangerous.
Innocent and naive woman.

Male flaws represented too.
Gender equality shown.

theme_arguments.name: Setting
arguments: Eden not merely a backdrop but active participant in the fall.

arguments: Tragedy.
Epic.

theme_arguments.name: Free will
arguments: Milton suggests that exercising your free will is worth losing paradise. Freedom is valuable, even if it creates the possibility of sin.
Temptation necessary for freedom: not a flaw in creation but genuine necessity.
True test of free will is to resist temptation.
Paradise constructed as perfect to emphasise the cost of free will gone wrong.
The outcome validates God's warning, proving divine authority is just and true.

theme_arguments.name: Hierarchy and order
arguments: Presents the fatal consequences of disobeying one's superior.
Disorder begins with separation and culminates in chaos.
Adam misuses his authority.
Eve's resistance can be seen as rational/admirable.

theme_arguments.name: Blame for the fall
arguments: Prelapsarian perfection vs postlapsarian lust — Eve's innocence caused the fall.
Eve never innocent to begin with — already capable of error.
Adam complicit through uxoriousness and abdication of authority.

theme_arguments.name: Ambition
arguments: Eve's ambition and agency drives her toward the fruit.
Satan's ambition — refusal to serve, will to overthrow.
Adam not ambitious — falls through love, not pride.

theme_arguments.name: Human flaws
arguments: Eve ambitious before she meets Satan — flaw is pre-existing.
Satan exploits her ambition rather than implanting it.
Adam's flaw is uxoriousness, not ambition.

theme_arguments.name: Satan
arguments: Human perfection: A+E perfect by definition / could never be perfect / already flawed before the fall / the fall exposes the illusion of perfection.
Satan as tragic hero — propels the epic action, grandeur and suffering.
Satan diminished — Milton ultimately undercuts any heroism.
Satan as necessary vehicle through which a providentially anticipated temptation is enacted.
Satan sympathised — psychological depth humanises him as displaced, alienated figure.

theme_arguments.name: Seduction
arguments: Satan's seduction — rhetorical campaign actively distorts Eve's moral framework.
Mutual seduction — Eve self-seduces, seduces Satan, then seduces Adam.
Milton's aesthetic seduction — the expansion of Genesis is itself a form of aesthetic and intellectual seduction.

theme_arguments.name: Sin
arguments: The allure of sin looks magnificent — Satan's grandeur, the fruit's beauty, the seductive rhetoric.
The consequences of sin — shame, discord, exile, death; postlapsarian lust replaces prelapsarian love.
Sin is a structural and theological necessity — without it no redemption, no free will, no fortunate fall.
